etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English dredful, dredfull, dredeful (also dreful), equivalent to dread +‎ -ful.

definitions.definition: Genuinely horrific, awful, or alarming; dangerous, risky.

quote.citation: 1900 May 17, L[yman] Frank Baum, chapter 23, in The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chicago, Ill.; New York, N.Y.: Geo[rge] M[elvin] Hill Co., →OCLC:
quote.text: "...Aunt Em will surely think something dreadful has happened to me, and that will make her put on mourning..."

definitions.definition: (hyperbolic) Unpleasant, awful, very bad (also used as an intensifier).

quote.citation: 1682, T. Creech's translation of Lucretius, De Natura Rerum, Book II, 52:
quote.text: Here some... Look dreadful gay in their own sparkling blood.

quote.citation: 1918, W[illiam] B[abington] Maxwell, chapter XVII, in The Mirror and the Lamp, Indianapolis, Ind.: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: This time was most dreadful for Lilian. Thrown on her own resources and almost penniless, she maintained herself and paid the rent of a wretched room near the hospital by working as a charwoman, sempstress, anything.

quote.citation: 2011 December 10, Marc Higginson, “Bolton 1-2 Aston Villa”, in BBC Sport:
quote.text: After a dreadful performance in the opening 45 minutes, they upped their game after the break...

definitions.definition: (obsolete) Awesome, awe-inspiring, causing feelings of reverence.
Full of something causing dread, whether

quote.citation: 1958, T[erence] H[anbury] White, chapter VIII, in The Once and Future King, New York, N.Y.: G. P. Putnam's Sons, →ISBN, book I (The Sword in the Stone):
quote.text: Shame to the slothful and woe to the weak one.Death to the dreadful who turn to flee.Blood to the tearing, the talon’d, the beaked one.Timor Mortis are We.

quote.citation: 2003, David Davis, Of Preachers and Pagans, page 199:
quote.text: I'm sorry, Miz Terrigan. I'm dreadful sorry.

quote.citation: 2007, Oliver Wendell Holmes, Professor At The Breakfast Table, page 130:
quote.text: You don't look so dreadful poor in the face as you did a while back.

quote.citation: 2015, Hesba Stretton, Jessica's first prayer: A Christian Fiction of Hesba Stretton:
quote.text: "No," she replied, coolly, "and I shall want my dinner dreadful bad afore I get it, I know. You don't often feel dreadful hungry, do you, sir?

definitions.definition: A shocker: a report of a crime written in a provokingly lurid style.
A journal or broadsheet printing such reports.
